question.text: Is vitamin D deficiency a feature of pediatric celiac disease?
question.context: Celiac disease (CD) is an autoimmune enteropathy characterized by villus atrophy and malabsorption of essential nutrients. Vitamin D deficiency has been described in autoimmune diseases, but its status in prepubertal children with CD has not been adequately studied. To determine the vitamin D status of prepubertal children with CD. A retrospective study of prepubertal children aged 3-12 years with CD (n=24) who were compared to prepubertal, non-CD children of the same age (n=50). Children were included in the study if they had a diagnosis of CD by intestinal biopsy, and were not on a gluten-free diet (GFD). Patients were excluded if they had diseases of calcium or vitamin D metabolism, or were receiving calcium or vitamin D supplementation or had other autoimmune diseases. All subjects had their serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] level measured. There was no difference in 25(OH)D level between the CD and non-CD children (27.58 +/- 9.91 versus 26.20 +/- 10.45, p = 0.59). However, when the patients were subdivided into obese and non-obese groups, the non-obese CD patients had a significantly higher 25(OH)D level than the obese normal children (28.39 +/- 10.26 versus 21.58 +/- 5.67, p = 0.009). In contrast, there was no difference in 25(OH)D level between non-obese CD patients and non-obese normal children (28.39 +/- 10.26 versus 30.64 +/-12.08, p = 0.52). The season of 25(OH)D measurement was not a significant confounder (p =0.7).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant difference in 25(OH)D levels between prepubertal children with celiac disease and a control group of non-CD children. While there was a trend towards higher vitamin D levels in non-obese CD patients compared to obese normal children, this difference was not statistically significant. Therefore, vitamin D deficiency is not a consistent feature of pediatric celiac disease.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: There was no difference in 25(OH)D level between the CD and non-CD children (27.58 +/- 9.91 versus 26.20 +/- 10.45, p = 0.59).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Other autoimmune diseases could potentially affect vitamin D levels, but the study excluded patients with diseases of calcium or vitamin D metabolism and other autoimmune diseases, making this less likely. Malabsorption could theoretically affect vitamin D, but the study focused on vitamin D levels and not the overall absorption of nutrients.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant difference in vitamin D levels between prepubertal children with celiac disease and those without, except when considering obesity. Since the question asks if vitamin D deficiency is a general feature of pediatric celiac disease, and the overall comparison showed no significant difference, the answer is no.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The p = 0.59 result showing no difference in 25(OH)D levels between CD and non-CD children
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: While obesity was a factor in the subgroup analysis, it was not the focus of the question. The study specifically compared CD and non-CD children of similar age and health status, making the overall result more relevant to the general question.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant difference in vitamin D levels between children with celiac disease and healthy controls overall. While obesity was associated with lower vitamin D in the control group, this did not translate to a deficiency in celiac disease patients, even when stratified by obesity status. Thus, vitamin D deficiency is not a defining feature of pediatric celiac disease in this cohort.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: There was no difference in 25(OH)D level between CD and non-CD children (27.58 ± 9.91 vs 26.20 ± 10.45, p = 0.59).
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Obesity was considered as a confounder, but the study showed that vitamin D levels in non-obese CD patients were not significantly different from non-obese controls, ruling out obesity as the primary driver of deficiency in CD.

olmo3_7b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant difference in vitamin D levels between children with celiac disease and those without, even when adjusting for obesity status. However, within the celiac disease group, non-obese patients had higher vitamin D levels than obese patients. This suggests that obesity may be associated with vitamin D deficiency in this population, but the overall prevalence of vitamin D deficiency in celiac disease is not significantly different from the general pediatric population. Therefore, it is not accurate to say that vitamin D deficiency is a feature of celiac disease as a whole, but obesity could be a modifying factor.
olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: The result showing no significant difference in 25(OH)D levels between CD and non-CD children (p=0.59), but a significant difference within the CD group between non-obese and obese patients (p=0.009), indicates that celiac disease itself is not inherently linked to vitamin D deficiency, though obesity may be a risk factor within the disease.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other causes of vitamin D deficiency (e.g., limited sun exposure, malnutrition unrelated to celiac, genetic factors affecting vitamin D metabolism) were not the main focus of the study, but the absence of a group-level difference in CD patients versus controls supports that celiac disease is not a feature for vitamin D deficiency overall.
